proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(X_Y(a)=(a,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_Y(a))\) for the data produced by schedule \(Y\) under assignment \(a\). The action in \texttt{def:pair-invariance-group} preserves the two discordance counts, the class \(\Theta_{J,s}\), and \(\tau\). This uses binary support from \(\texttt{ass:binary-outcome-support}\) and the two inequalities in \(\texttt{ass:armwise-discordance-budget}\). Given an admissible procedure \((Q,\delta)\), define
\[
 \bar Q(a)=|G_J|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G_J}Q(g^{-1}a).
\]
Outcome independence in \(\texttt{ass:design-exogeneity}\) makes \(\bar Q\) an admissible ex ante law. If \(\bar Q(a)>0\), put
\[
 w_g(a)=\frac{Q(g^{-1}a)}{\sum_{u\in G_J}Q(u^{-1}a)},\qquad
 \bar\delta\{X_Y(a)\}=\sum_{g\in G_J}w_g(a)\delta\{g^{-1}X_Y(a)\};
\]
on a \(\bar Q\)-null assignment choose any value in \([-1,1]\). This is a deterministic measurable function of the observed data: the weights use only \(a\) and the fixed design. Generate the symmetrized experiment by drawing \(g\) uniformly, drawing \(b\sim Q\), and setting \(a=gb\). Conditional expectation over \(g\) gives \(\bar\delta\). Since squared loss is convex and \(\tau(g^{-1}Y)=\tau(Y)\), Jensen's inequality gives
\[
 \mathcal R_{J,s}(\bar Q,\bar\delta;Y)
 \le |G_J|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G_J}\mathcal R_{J,s}(Q,\delta;g^{-1}Y)
 \le \sup_{Y'\in\Theta_{J,s}}\mathcal R_{J,s}(Q,\delta;Y').
\]
Thus invariant procedures are lossless. Conversely, an invariant assignment law is uniform inside each assignment orbit and is specified by \(q\), while an invariant estimator is specified by \(\eta_{no}\).

There are
\[
 |\mathcal N_J|={J+2\choose2},\qquad
 |\mathcal H_{J,s}|\le {J+9\choose9},\qquad
 |\mathcal O_J|={J+9\choose9}.
\]
To verify the kernel rather than assume it, choose a list \(t_1,\ldots,t_J\) containing \(h_t\) copies of each \(t\). Let \(M_0(0,0)=1\), with all other entries zero, and recursively set
\[
 M_{k+1}(n,o)=\sum_{a\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{loc}}}
 M_k\bigl(n-e_{\nu(a)},o-e_{\omega(t_{k+1},a)}\bigr),
\]
where a term with a negative coordinate is zero. Induction on \(k\) shows that \(M_k(n,o)\) counts the local assignments of the first \(k\) pairs having marks \((n,o)\). Hence \(M_J(n,o)\) is the coefficient in \(F_h\). Exactly \(C_n\) labelled assignments have orbit \(n\), so
\[
 K_{hno}=M_J(n,o)/C_n,\qquad \sum_oK_{hno}=1.
\]
This proves the asserted observation law. The rectangular array has at most
\[
 {J+9\choose9}^{\!2}{J+2\choose2}=O(J^{20})
\]
entries. Both \(M_J(n,o)\) and \(C_n\) lie between zero and \(4^J\), apart from the strictly positive denominator, so every reduced rational entry has numerator and denominator of \(O(J)\) bits. The displayed recurrence computes every entry using integer additions.

It remains to derive the game and its certificate. Put \(t_{no}=q_n\eta_{no}\). On
\[
 \mathcal P_{\mathrm{pr}}=\{(q,t):q_n\ge0,\ \sum_nq_n=1,\ -q_n\le t_{no}\le q_n\},
\]
use the closed perspective convention
\[
 q_nK_{hno}(\eta_{no}-\tau_h)^2
 =K_{hno}\frac{(t_{no}-q_n\tau_h)^2}{q_n},
\]
with value zero at \((q_n,t_{no})=(0,0)\). The expression is convex and continuous on \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{pr}}\), because its absolute value is at most \(4K_{hno}q_n\) near \(q_n=0\). Thus \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{pr}}\) is a compact convex representation of all invariant procedures. Since the maximum over \(h\) equals the maximum over priors \(\pi\), the cited Sion minimax lemma applies and yields
\[
 \min_{(q,t)\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{pr}}}\max_{\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal H_{J,s})}
 \sum_h\pi_h\mathcal R_h(q,t/q)
 =\max_{\pi}\min_{(q,t)\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{pr}}}
 \sum_h\pi_h\mathcal R_h(q,t/q).
\]
For a fixed \(\pi\), define also \(d_{no}(\pi)=\sum_h\pi_hK_{hno}\tau_h^2\). The contribution of cell \((n,o)\) to prior risk is
\[
 a_{no}(\pi)t_{no}^2/q_n-2c_{no}(\pi)t_{no}+q_nd_{no}(\pi).
\]
If \(a_{no}>0\), its minimum occurs at \(t_{no}=q_nc_{no}/a_{no}\); this is feasible because \(c_{no}/a_{no}\) is a convex combination of numbers \(\tau_h\in[-1,1]\). If \(a_{no}=0\), then \(c_{no}=d_{no}=0\). Consequently
\[
 \min_t\sum_h\pi_h\mathcal R_h(q,t/q)
 =\sum_nq_n\left\{\sum_h\pi_h\tau_h^2-
 \sum_{o:a_{no}>0}\frac{c_{no}^2}{a_{no}}\right\}
 =\sum_nq_nB_n(\pi).
\]
Minimizing over the simplex in \(q\) gives \(\min_nB_n(\pi)\), proving both displayed equalities and attainment.

If \(q\in\mathcal Q^*(J,s)\), choose an attaining \(\eta\), an attaining dual prior \(\pi\), and \(v=R^*(J,s)\). Primal feasibility gives \(\mathcal R_h(q,\eta)\le v\) for all \(h\), while dual optimality gives \(B_n(\pi)\ge v\) for all \(n\). Conversely, the two displayed families of inequalities imply
\[
 R^*(J,s)\le\max_h\mathcal R_h(q,\eta)\le v
 \le\min_nB_n(\pi)\le R^*(J,s),
\]
so equality holds throughout and \(q\in\mathcal Q^*(J,s)\). Fixing \(q=q^{\mathrm{pair}}\), \(q=q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\), or \(q\in\mathcal C_J\) gives the stated membership and noncanonicality tests. Finally, the perspective formulation has a compact convex optimal set; projecting it onto its \(q\)-coordinates gives exactly \(\mathcal Q^*(J,s)\). Optimizing each coordinate \(q_n\) over that projection decides singleton uniqueness: the projection is a singleton if and only if every coordinate's minimum equals its maximum.

By \texttt{def:bounded-mismatch-class}, the inequalities \(D_a(Y)\le s\le s'\) imply
\[
 \Theta_{J,s}\subseteq\Theta_{J,s'}.
\]
The design and estimator classes are otherwise unchanged, so taking a supremum over the larger schedule class and then the same infimum gives \(R^*(J,s)\le R^*(J,s')\).

Suppose first that \(s=0\). Then each pair is homogeneous in each arm. Under \(q^{\mathrm{pair}}\), define the observable estimator
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm{pair}}
 =\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^J\sum_{r=1}^2
 \{A_{jr}Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_{jr}-(1-A_{jr})Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_{jr}\}.
\]
Exactly one unit per pair is treated, and homogeneity makes the treated observation equal the pair's common treatment potential outcome and the control observation equal its common control potential outcome. Therefore \(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{pair}}=\tau(Y)\) for every \(Y\in\Theta_{J,0}\), so nonnegativity of squared loss gives \(R^*(J,0)=0\).

For uniqueness among invariant orbit laws, suppose \(q_n>0\) for an orbit \(n\ne(0,0,J)\). Every assignment in that orbit has an unmixed pair. Fix one such assignment \(a\) and pair \(j\). If pair \(j\) is all control, take two schedules in \(\Theta_{J,0}\) that are zero everywhere except that the second schedule has both treatment potential outcomes in pair \(j\) equal to one. They give identical observations under \(a\), but their SATEs differ by \(1/J\). If pair \(j\) is all treated, make the analogous change to its two control potential outcomes. A single estimator value cannot equal both targets. Since the invariant law assigns probability \(q_n/C_n>0\) to \(a\), at least one of the two schedules has positive risk. Thus zero worst-case risk forces support only on \((0,0,J)\), proving \(\mathcal Q^*(J,0)=\{q^{\mathrm{pair}}\}\).

At \(s=J\), both discordance inequalities are vacuous, hence
\[
 \Theta_{J,J}=\{0,1\}^{\mathcal P_J\times\{0,1\}},
 \qquad R^*(J,J)=r^{\mathrm U}_{2J}
\]
by the two minimax definitions. The cited unrestricted binary theorem states that independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment and its nonlinear least-favourable-prior Bayes rule attain this value. Its orbit masses are \(C_n/4^J=q_n^{\mathrm{Ber}}\). The invariant reduction of Theorem 1 therefore places \(q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\) in \(\mathcal Q^*(J,J)\), with the asserted posterior-mean estimator.

Under \(q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\), the six orbit masses in the displayed order are
\[
 (1/4,1/4,1/16,1/4,1/8,1/16).
\]
If \(q^{\mathrm U}=\lambda q^{\mathrm{pair}}+(1-\lambda)q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\), its last coordinate \(1/100\) would give \(1-\lambda=4/25\). Its second coordinate would then be \(1/25\), whereas the displayed second coordinate of \(q^{\mathrm U}\) is \(3/10\). Hence \(q^{\mathrm U}\notin\mathcal C_2\).

We next give the exact arithmetic check. Number the ten local schedule types lexicographically by \(0,\ldots,9\), and number the 38 feasible two-pair multisets lexicographically by their ordered type-index pairs. Applying the integer coefficient recurrence in Theorem 1 to the displayed rational vectors \(q^{\mathrm U}\), \(\pi^{\mathrm U}\), and \(\pi^{\mathrm H}\), with zero used precisely on cells having \(a_{no}=0\), gives
\[
 \max_{h\in\mathcal H_{2,1}}\mathcal R_h(q^{\mathrm U},\eta^{\mathrm U})
 =\frac{3850693539551962000276103702569949405421799518612146614194263925096941}
 {42480492487647577202373742417068406183238423509974554343379909221067500}.
\]
The maximum is attained at histogram index \(20\), whose two local types have indices \(3\) and \(7\); direct subtraction gives
\[
 \frac{9065}{100000}-\max_h\mathcal R_h(q^{\mathrm U},\eta^{\mathrm U})
 =\frac{1304835626326984952608380298412920710108580536373896264998766342623}
 {339843939901180617618989939336547249465907388079796434747039273768540000}>0.
\]
The same recurrence and the definition of \(B\) give
\[
 B_{(0,0,2)}(\pi^{\mathrm H})
 =\frac{1120490298829500754077}{12309527381808500000000},
\]
and
\[
 \sum_nq_n^{\mathrm{Ber}}B_n(\pi^{\mathrm H})
 =\frac{1760496146710770175939617592960855471947446378734932636964736609}
 {19340529328385758315873504820452091980056895966176036468000000000}.
\]
Their respective excesses over \(9102/100000\) are
\[
 \frac{77116537291084077}{12309527381808500000000}>0
\]
and
\[
 \frac{121167241098454028811184203306059922667707893589797647376609}
 {19340529328385758315873504820452091980056895966176036468000000000}>0.
\]
All denominators displayed above are positive, so these are exact strict certificates, not floating-point comparisons.

For \(q_\lambda=\lambda q^{\mathrm{pair}}+(1-\lambda)q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\) and any estimator \(\eta\), maximum risk dominates Bayes risk under \(\pi^{\mathrm H}\), which in turn dominates the optimized Bayes risk. The cellwise calculation in Theorem 1 therefore gives
\[
 \max_h\mathcal R_h(q_\lambda,\eta)
 \ge \lambda B_{(0,0,2)}(\pi^{\mathrm H})
 +(1-\lambda)\sum_nq_n^{\mathrm{Ber}}B_n(\pi^{\mathrm H})
 >\frac{9102}{100000}.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(\lambda\) and \(\eta\) proves the canonical lower bound. The unrestricted optimum is at most the certified risk of \((q^{\mathrm U},\eta^{\mathrm U})\), so no canonical law can be optimal. Finally,
\[
 \frac{9102}{100000}-\frac{9065}{100000}=\frac{37}{100000},
\]
and both preceding inequalities are strict, proving the asserted all-estimator gap.

For paired randomization, let \(H_j=2A_{j1}-1\), so the \(H_j\) are independent Rademacher variables, and put \(\mu_{jr}=\{Y_{jr}(1)+Y_{jr}(0)\}/2\). The observable paired difference estimator satisfies
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm P}-\tau(Y)
 =\frac1J\sum_{j=1}^JH_j(\mu_{j1}-\mu_{j2}).
\]
It takes values in \([-1,1]\). Independence and mean zero give
\[
 \mathbb E(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm P}-\tau)^2
 =\frac1{J^2}\sum_j(\mu_{j1}-\mu_{j2})^2
 \le\frac1{2J^2}\sum_j\sum_{a=0}^1
 \{Y_{j1}(a)-Y_{j2}(a)\}^2
 \le\frac{s}{J^2}.
\]
The first inequality is \((x+y)^2\le2(x^2+y^2)\), and the second uses binary support and each discordance bound.

Under independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment define the observable centered estimator
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm B}=\frac1{2J}\sum_{j,r}(2A_{jr}-1)(2Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_{jr}-1).
\]
It also lies in \([-1,1]\). With \(v_{jr}=Y_{jr}(1)+Y_{jr}(0)-1\in\{-1,0,1\}\), direct substitution gives
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm B}-\tau(Y)=\frac1{2J}\sum_{j,r}(2A_{jr}-1)v_{jr},
\]
and independence yields
\[
 \mathbb E(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm B}-\tau)^2
 =\frac1{4J^2}\sum_{j,r}v_{jr}^2\le\frac1{2J}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 R^*(J,s)\le\min\{s/J^2,1/(2J)\}.
\]

We prove the matching lower bound without introducing superpopulation randomness into the target: the following random schedule is only a Bayes device for lower-bounding the supremum over fixed schedules. Fix \(0<r<\min\{\rho,1/2\}\), let \(b_J=J^{-1/4}\), and let \(\theta\) have density \(b_J^{-1}w(\theta/b_J)\), where \(w\) is continuously differentiable, is supported on \([-1,1]\), vanishes at both endpoints, and has finite Fisher information \(I_w\). Conditional on \(\theta\), draw the pairs independently from the following five types:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
\text{type}&H_0&H_1&D&E_+&E_-\\ \hline
\text{probability}&(1-r-2b_J)/2&(1-r-2b_J)/2&r&b_J+\theta/2&b_J-\theta/2.
\end{array}
\]
Here \(H_y\) has both units of no-effect type \((y,y)\), \(D\) contains one \((0,0)\) and one \((1,1)\) unit with uniform orientation, and \(E_+\) and \(E_-\) have two copies of \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\), respectively. All probabilities are positive for large \(J\). If \(\tau_J\) denotes the realized finite-population SATE, then
\[
 \mathbb E(\tau_J\mid\theta)=\theta,\qquad
 \mathbb E\{(\tau_J-\theta)^2\mid\theta\}
 =\frac{2b_J-\theta^2}{J}\le\frac{2b_J}{J}.
\]

For a fixed assignment, pairs are conditionally independent. A mixed pair has two \(\theta\)-informative observation probabilities \((r+2b_J+\theta)/2\) and \((r+2b_J-\theta)/2\), so its Fisher information is
\[
 I_{\mathrm m}(\theta)=\frac{r+2b_J}{(r+2b_J)^2-\theta^2}.
\]
An all-treated or all-control pair has two informative probabilities \((1-r+\theta)/2\) and \((1-r-\theta)/2\), up to interchange, and hence information
\[
 I_{\mathrm s}(\theta)=\frac{1-r}{(1-r)^2-\theta^2}.
\]
Uniformly on \(|\theta|\le b_J\), these are at most \(1/r+o(1)\), because \(r<1/2\). Assignment is independent of the schedule by \(\texttt{ass:design-exogeneity}\), so every design has total expected information at most \(J/r+o(J)\). The prior information is \(I_w/b_J^2=o(J)\). The cited scalar van Trees inequality therefore gives, for every estimator,
\[
 \mathbb E(\delta-\theta)^2\ge\frac{r+o(1)}J.
\]
Minkowski's inequality and the displayed empirical-target variance imply
\[
 \{\mathbb E(\delta-\tau_J)^2\}^{1/2}
 \ge \{\mathbb E(\delta-\theta)^2\}^{1/2}
 -\{2b_J/J\}^{1/2},
\]
and therefore \(\mathbb E(\delta-\tau_J)^2\ge\{r+o(1)\}/J\).

Only the \(D\) pairs are discordant, in both arms. Their number \(N_D\) is \(\operatorname{Binomial}(J,r)\) and is independent of \(\theta\). For \(C_J=\{N_D\le s_J\}\), Markov's inequality applied to \(e^{\lambda N_D}\) gives
\[
 \Pr(C_J^c)\le e^{-\lambda s_J}(1-r+re^\lambda)^J=e^{-cJ}
\]
for some fixed \(\lambda,c>0\), since \(r<\rho\). Squared loss is at most four. If \(L\) and \(L_C\) are its Bayes risks before and after conditioning on \(C_J\), then
\[
 L\le \Pr(C_J)L_C+4\Pr(C_J^c),
\]
so \(L_C\ge\{r+o(1)\}/J\). This conditioned prior is supported on \(\Theta_{J,s_J}\); hence \(R^*(J,s_J)\ge\{r+o(1)\}/J\). Letting \(r\uparrow\min\{\rho,1/2\}\), and combining with the upper bound (with the case \(\rho=0\) supplied by nonnegativity), proves
\[
 JR^*(J,s_J)\longrightarrow\min\{\rho,1/2\}.
\]

We now prove the design concentration when \(0<\rho<1/2\). Conditional on an assignment orbit \(n\), write \(m_n=n_{\mathrm m}/J\). The same scalar prior has total leading information
\[
 J\left\{\frac{m_n}{r}+\frac{1-m_n}{1-r}\right\},
\]
uniformly in \(n\). The preceding van Trees, transfer, and hard-budget conditioning steps, now performed conditional on \(n\), imply for any optimal orbit law \(q_J\)
\[
 JR^*(J,s_J)\ge\sum_nq_{J,n}g_r(m_n)+o(1),
 \qquad
 g_r(m)=\left\{\frac m r+\frac{1-m}{1-r}\right\}^{-1}.
\]
If \(\mu\) is a weak accumulation point, continuity of \(g_r\) and the already proved value limit give
\[
 \int g_r(m)\,d\mu\le\rho\qquad(0<r<\rho).
\]
Letting \(r\uparrow\rho\) gives \(\int g_\rho(m)\,d\mu\le\rho\). Since \(\rho<1/2\), \(g_\rho(m)\ge\rho\), with equality only at \(m=1\). Thus \(\mu=\delta_{(0,0,1)}\).

When \(\rho=0\), use instead a prior supported on \(\Theta_{J,0}\subseteq\Theta_{J,s_J}\): independently across pairs and arms, draw homogeneous pair values \(Z_{ja}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\). Conditional on orbit \(n\), a mixed pair reveals both \(Z_{j0},Z_{j1}\), whereas an unmixed pair leaves one independent Bernoulli value missing. The posterior variance of SATE is exactly
\[
 \frac{J-n_{\mathrm m}}{4J^2}.
\]
Thus optimality implies \(JR^*(J,s_J)\ge\sum_nq_{J,n}(1-m_n)/4\). The left side tends to zero, so every accumulation point has \(m=1\) almost surely and is again \(\delta_{(0,0,1)}\). Compactness of \(\Delta_2\) and uniqueness of the accumulation point give weak convergence of the full sequence. Finally, for the Euclidean metric the only coupling of \(\mu_{q_J}\) with the point mass at \(x_0=(0,0,1)\) gives
\[
 W_1(\mu_{q_J},\delta_{x_0})=\int\|x-x_0\|\,d\mu_{q_J}(x)\longrightarrow0
\]
by weak convergence and bounded continuity of the integrand. This proves the stated equivalent \(W_1\) conclusion.

Let \(v_J=\max_h\mathcal R_h(q_J,\eta_J)\). Theorem 4 gives \(Jv_J\to1/2\). We first derive all necessary restrictions on a weak accumulation point \(\mu\).

Fix \(r\in(0,\rho)\), taking \(r<1/2\) when \(\rho=1/2\), and again let \(b=b_J\downarrow0\) with \(Jb^2\to\infty\). Give \((\theta,\phi)\) independent smooth scaled priors on \([-b,b]\), each vanishing at its boundary and having Fisher information \(O(b^{-2})\). Conditional on \((\theta,\phi)\), draw pair types independently with probabilities
\[
 \frac{1-r-2b-\phi}{2},\quad
 \frac{1-r-2b+\phi}{2},\quad
 r,\quad b+\frac\theta2,\quad b-\frac\theta2
\]
for \(H_0,H_1,D,E_+,E_-\), respectively. These probabilities are positive for large \(J\). As before,
\[
 \mathbb E(\tau_J\mid\theta,\phi)=\theta,\qquad
 \mathbb E\{(\tau_J-\theta)^2\mid\theta,\phi\}\le2b/J,
\]
and the number of discordant pairs is \(\operatorname{Binomial}(J,r)\), independent of \((\theta,\phi)\).

For parameter order \((\theta,\phi)\), the exact information matrices of a mixed, all-treated, and all-control pair are, respectively,
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \dfrac{r+2b}{(r+2b)^2-\theta^2}&0\\[4pt]
 0&\dfrac{1-r-2b}{(1-r-2b)^2-\phi^2}
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
 \frac{1-r}{(1-r)^2-(\theta+\phi)^2}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \frac{1-r}{(1-r)^2-(\phi-\theta)^2}
 \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
These follow by summing \((\nabla p)(\nabla p)^\top/p\) over the three observable outcome categories. Therefore, conditional on an orbit whose normalized coordinates are \(x=(x_{00},x_{11},m)\) and with \(d=x_{11}-x_{00}\), the information divided by \(J\) converges uniformly on the prior support to
\[
 M_r(m,d)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \dfrac m r+\dfrac{1-m}{1-r}&\dfrac d{1-r}\\[5pt]
 \dfrac d{1-r}&\dfrac1{1-r}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its Schur complement for estimating \(\theta\) in the presence of nuisance \(\phi\) is
\[
 S_r(m,d)=\frac m r+\frac{1-m-d^2}{1-r}.
\]
Feasibility of \(x\in\Delta_2\) gives \(|d|\le1-m\), so \(S_r\ge0\), and it is positive except at the nonidentified endpoints \((m,d)=(0,\pm1)\).

Apply the cited matrix van Trees inequality conditionally on each assignment orbit and then use the same empirical-SATE transfer and exponentially small hard-budget conditioning as in Theorem 4. The prior information divided by \(J\) is \(O((Jb^2)^{-1})\to0\). At nonsingular points, the first diagonal entry of \(M_r^{-1}\) is
\[
 g_r(m,d)=S_r(m,d)^{-1}
 =\left\{\frac m r+\frac{1-m-d^2}{1-r}\right\}^{-1}.
\]
At a singular endpoint set \(g_r=+\infty\). This passage is also valid under varying orbit laws: adding \(\varepsilon I_2\) to \(M_r\) gives continuous finite lower bounds, the exact information converges uniformly, and then \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\); monotone convergence handles the singular endpoints. Hence, along any subsequence with \(\mu_{q_J}\Rightarrow\mu\),
\[
 \int g_r(m,d)\,d\mu\le\liminf_JJv_J=\frac12.
\]

If \(\rho>1/2\), take \(r=1/2\); if \(\rho=1/2\), take \(r\uparrow1/2\) and use Fatou's lemma. In both cases,
\[
 \int\frac1{2(1-d^2)}\,d\mu\le\frac12.
\]
The integrand is at least \(1/2\), with equality exactly when \(d=0\), so \(\mu\{d=0\}=1\). On that line define
\[
 G_\mu(r)=\int\left\{\frac m r+\frac{1-m}{1-r}\right\}^{-1}d\mu.
\]
For \(r\) near \(1/2\), bounded differentiation under the integral gives
\[
 G_\mu(1/2)=1/2,\qquad G_\mu'(1/2)=\int(2m-1)\,d\mu=2\int m\,d\mu-1.
\]
At \(\rho=1/2\), the inequality \(G_\mu(r)\le1/2\) is available for \(r<1/2\), so the left derivative is nonnegative and \(\int m\,d\mu\ge1/2\). If \(\rho>1/2\), it is available on both sides of \(1/2\), so the derivative is zero and \(\int m\,d\mu=1/2\). These are exactly the defining conditions of \(\mathcal F_\rho\).

For sufficiency, let \(\mu\in\mathcal F_\rho\). The balanced finite-orbit grid is
\[
 E_J=\{(k/J,k/J,1-2k/J):0\le k\le\lfloor J/2\rfloor\}.
\]
It becomes dense in the line \(d=0\). Rounding points on that line to adjacent elements of \(E_J\), and splitting mass between adjacent points whenever they bracket the original point, produces laws supported on balanced orbits that converge weakly to \(\mu\) and whose mean mixed fraction differs from \(\int m\,d\mu\) by at most \(2/J\). If that limiting mean is \(1/2\), transfer \(O(J^{-1})\) total mass between the two extreme grid points to make the finite mean exactly \(1/2\); this perturbation preserves weak convergence. If the limiting mean is strictly above \(1/2\), the rounded mean is above \(1/2\) for all large \(J\). Thus we obtain orbit laws \(q_J\) for which
\[
 \bar m_J=\sum_nq_{J,n}n_{\mathrm m}/J=1/2
 \quad\text{if }\rho>1/2,
 \qquad
 \bar m_J\ge1/2
 \quad\text{if }\rho=1/2.
\]

Use the centered observable estimator
\[
 \widehat\tau_J=\frac1{2J}\sum_{j,r}(2A_{jr}-1)(2Y^{\mathrm{obs}}_{jr}-1).
\]
For \(S_{jr}=2A_{jr}-1\), balance of every supported orbit gives \(\mathbb ES_{jr}=0\). Invariance and the deterministic identity \(\sum_{j,r}S_{jr}=0\) on each balanced orbit give
\[
 c_{\mathrm w}:=\mathbb E(S_{j1}S_{j2})=1-2\bar m_J,\qquad
 c_{\mathrm b}:=\mathbb E(S_{jr}S_{k\ell})=-\frac{1-\bar m_J}{J-1}\quad(j\ne k).
\]
With \(v_{jr}=Y_{jr}(1)+Y_{jr}(0)-1\) and \(w_j=v_{j1}+v_{j2}\), direct expansion yields
\[
 4J^2\mathbb E(\widehat\tau_J-\tau)^2
 =\sum_j\{v_{j1}^2+v_{j2}^2+2c_{\mathrm w}v_{j1}v_{j2}\}
 +c_{\mathrm b}\left\{\left(\sum_jw_j\right)^2-\sum_jw_j^2\right\}.
\]
Because \(c_{\mathrm b}\le0\) and \(w_j^2\le4\), the second term is at most \(-c_{\mathrm b}\sum_jw_j^2=O(1)\), uniformly in the schedule. Since \(c_{\mathrm w}\le0\), checking the four binary unit types gives, pair by pair,
\[
 v_{j1}^2+v_{j2}^2+2c_{\mathrm w}v_{j1}v_{j2}
 \le2(1+c_{\mathrm w})-2c_{\mathrm w}
 \sum_{a=0}^1\mathbf 1\{Y_{j1}(a)\ne Y_{j2}(a)\}.
\]
Summing and using \(D_0(Y)+D_1(Y)\le2s_J\) gives
\[
 \sup_{h\in\mathcal H_{J,s_J}}\mathcal R_h(q_J,\widehat\tau_J)
 \le\frac{1+c_{\mathrm w}(1-2s_J/J)}{2J}+O(J^{-2}).
\]
If \(\rho>1/2\), then \(c_{\mathrm w}=0\). If \(\rho=1/2\), then \(-1\le c_{\mathrm w}\le0\) and \(1-2s_J/J=o(1)\). In either case the right side is \(1/(2J)+o(J^{-1})\). Theorem 4 says \(R^*(J,s_J)=1/(2J)+o(J^{-1})\), while the minimax value is no larger than this procedure's worst risk. Therefore
\[
 \max_h\mathcal R_h(q_J,\widehat\tau_J)=R^*(J,s_J)+o(J^{-1}),
\]
and \(\mu_{q_J}\Rightarrow\mu\), completing the recovery proof.

Fix \(Y\in\Theta_{J,s}\), let \(h_Y\in\mathcal H_{J,s}\) be its schedule orbit, and put \(t_0=\tau(Y)=\tau_{h_Y}\). By the coefficient-counting proof in Theorem 1, under the invariant design the probability of cell \((n,o)\) is \(q_nK_{h_Yno}\). For this simple schedule-orbit null define
\[
 p_{h_Y}(n,o)=\sum_{n',o'}q_{n'}K_{h_Yn'o'}
 \mathbf 1\{T_{t_0}(n',o')\ge T_{t_0}(n,o)\}.
\]
This tail value is superuniform. Indeed, order the finitely many distinct values of \(T_{t_0}\) from largest to smallest and let \(S_k\) be the cumulative probability through level \(k\). Every cell at level \(k\) has \(p_{h_Y}=S_k\), so the union of levels satisfying \(S_k\le\alpha\) has probability equal to its largest such cumulative probability and is at most \(\alpha\). Thus
\[
 \Pr_{h_Y,q}\{p_{h_Y}(n(A),o(A,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}))\le\alpha\}\le\alpha.
\]

Every realized cell has \(K_{h_Yno}>0\) almost surely. Therefore the maximization in \(p_{t_0}\) contains the true orbit \(h_Y\), and
\[
 p_{t_0}(n,o)\ge p_{h_Y}(n,o).
\]
Using the strict acceptance rule in \texttt{def:exact-confidence-set},
\[
 \Pr\{\tau(Y)\notin\mathcal C_{\alpha,s}\}
 =\Pr\{p_{t_0}(n(A),o(A,Y^{\mathrm{obs}}))\le\alpha\}
 \le\alpha.
\]
This proves the claimed coverage. The interval hull contains the confidence set, so it has at least the same coverage.

The target grid has \(4J+1\) points, all feasible schedule nulls are among the already enumerated histograms, and every tail probability is a finite sum of entries \(q_nK_{hno}\). Hence the set and its hull use the same \(O(J^{20})\)-entry rational kernel as Theorem 1. No factorization of \(q\) was used, so arbitrary correlated and essentially noncanonical invariant laws are covered. Repeating the argument separately for each analyst-selected \(s\) gives the sensitivity family. Coverage is pointwise in \(s\); the proof uses no inclusion relation between procedures or acceptance regions at different values of \(s\), so it makes no nesting assertion.

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(X\) and \(Z\) be compact convex sets and let \(f:X\times Z\to\mathbb R\) be lower semicontinuous and convex in its first argument and upper semicontinuous and concave in its second argument. Then
\[
 \min_{x\in X}\max_{z\in Z}f(x,z)=\max_{z\in Z}\min_{x\in X}f(x,z),
\]
and both extrema are attained.

attestation.note: Specialized from Sion, On general minimax theorems, Theorem 3.4; the stable DOI and publisher PDF are supplied instead of a long verbatim transcription.
The displayed scalar-functional specialization is taken from Gill and Levit, Applications of the van Trees Inequality, Theorem 1; the stable DOI is supplied instead of a long verbatim transcription.

added_lemmas.statement: In the unrestricted fixed-population problem on \(2J\) units with potential outcomes in a known bounded interval, minimization over all assignment laws and all measurable estimators is attained by independent \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) assignment together with the nonlinear Bayes rule generated by a least-favourable endpoint prior. In particular, for binary outcomes this procedure attains \(r^{\mathrm U}_{2J}\).

attestation.note: Verified against the theorem and proof location in arXiv:2608.09812v3; the node records only the binary fixed-population specialization used here.

proposed.statement:
Theorem 1. For every \(J\ge2\) and \(0\le s\le J\), averaging over \(G_J\) is lossless for the minimax problem. The full rectangular kernel has \(O(J^{20})\) rational entries of \(O(J)\) bit length and is exactly computable by coefficient recursion from \(F_h\). Moreover,
\[
 R^*(J,s)=\min_{q,\eta}\max_{h\in\mathcal H_{J,s}}\sum_{n,o}q_nK_{hno}(\eta_{no}-\tau_h)^2
 =\max_{\pi\in\Delta(\mathcal H_{J,s})}\min_{n\in\mathcal N_J}B_n(\pi).
\]
An orbit law \(q\) belongs to \(\mathcal Q^*(J,s)\) if and only if there exist \(\eta\), \(\pi\), and \(v\) such that \(\mathcal R_h(q,\eta)\le v\) for every \(h\) and \(B_n(\pi)\ge v\) for every \(n\). This certificate decides membership of \(q^{\mathrm{pair}}\), \(q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\), and \(\mathcal C_J\), essential noncanonicality, and singleton uniqueness by coordinate optimization over the projected optimal face.
proposed.justification: The full primal--dual contact system, rather than the value alone, is needed to distinguish canonical and correlated minimax designs.
proposed.gap: Bai2023WhyRandomize gives the averaging move, SudijonoDobribanTchetgen2026 gives a scalar unrestricted game, and Kallus2021Optimality gives fixed-estimator mixed-strategy geometry; none gives this hard-budget all-estimator face.
proposed.consumer: For each analyst-selected sensitivity value \(s\), a trial designer can enumerate the exact minimax assignment laws and select one satisfying operational support or balance constraints without losing minimaxity for \(\Theta_{J,s}\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the published compact convex minimax theorem used in the primal--dual interchange.

proposed.statement: Proposition 2. If \(0\le s\le s'\le J\), then \(\Theta_{J,s}\subseteq\Theta_{J,s'}\) and \(R^*(J,s)\le R^*(J,s')\). At \(s=0\), \(R^*(J,0)=0\) and \(\mathcal Q^*(J,0)=\{q^{\mathrm{pair}}\}\). At \(s=J\), \(R^*(J,J)=r^{\mathrm U}_{2J}\), and \(q^{\mathrm{Ber}}\in\mathcal Q^*(J,J)\) with the nonlinear posterior-mean rule from the unrestricted binary experiment.
proposed.justification: The endpoints are mandatory reductions: perfect pair agreement makes paired assignment exact, while a vacuous budget recovers the published unrestricted problem.
proposed.gap: Bai2022MatchedPairs and Hull2026BoundedOutcomes motivate opposite endpoint prescriptions under different information classes; this proposition embeds both endpoints in one fixed-population model.
proposed.consumer: Analysts obtain a monotone worst-case-risk sensitivity curve in \(s\), with familiar paired and Bernoulli procedures anchoring its two endpoints; the optimal face itself is recomputed at each sensitivity value.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the published unrestricted binary minimax theorem used at the vacuous-budget endpoint.

proposed.statement:
Theorem 4. For every budget sequence with \(s_J/J\to\rho\in[0,1]\),
\[
 \lim_{J\to\infty}J R^*(J,s_J)=\min\{\rho,1/2\}.
\]
If \(0\le\rho<1/2\), then every sequence \(q_J\in\mathcal Q^*(J,s_J)\) satisfies \(\mu_{q_J}\Rightarrow\delta_{(0,0,1)}\), equivalently convergence holds in \(W_1\) on \(\Delta_2\).
proposed.justification: The formula quantifies the exact robustness value of pairing and identifies the phase boundary where first-order risk stops selecting the design.
proposed.gap: SudijonoDobribanTchetgen2026 and Hull2026BoundedOutcomes give the unrestricted endpoint constant, while Bai2022MatchedPairs gives a paired prescription under another criterion; no source derives this interpolation or concentration theorem.
proposed.consumer: The curve maps an analyst-selected discordance fraction to the sharp first-order sample-size cost and identifies when the minimax design must concentrate asymptotically on mixed pairs.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the scalar van Trees result used to derive, rather than assume, the sharp minimax lower bound and conditional-orbit concentration inequality.

proposed.statement: Theorem 5. Suppose \(s_J/J\to\rho\ge1/2\). Let \((q_J,\eta_J)_{J\ge2}\) be any sequence of invariant procedures satisfying \(\max_{h\in\mathcal H_{J,s_J}}\mathcal R_h(q_J,\eta_J)=R^*(J,s_J)+o(J^{-1})\), and let \(\mu_{q_J}=q_J\circ\{n\mapsto(n_{00}/J,n_{11}/J,n_{\mathrm m}/J)\}^{-1}\). With \(\mathcal P(\Delta_2)\) endowed with the weak topology, every weak accumulation point \(\mu\) of the sequence \((\mu_{q_J})_{J\ge2}\) lies in \(\mathcal F_\rho\). Conversely, for every measure \(\mu\in\mathcal F_\rho\), there exists a sequence of invariant procedures \((q_J,\eta_J)_{J\ge2}\) such that \(\mu_{q_J}\Rightarrow\mu\) and \(\max_{h\in\mathcal H_{J,s_J}}\mathcal R_h(q_J,\eta_J)=R^*(J,s_J)+o(J^{-1})\).
proposed.justification: This theorem identifies exactly why the leading minimax value cannot by itself determine limits of exact finite optimizers.
proposed.gap: HarshawSavjeSpielmanZhang2024 gives covariance guarantees for one estimator and SudijonoDobribanTchetgen2026 separates first- and second-order risk in another model; neither characterizes this measure-valued first-order face.
proposed.consumer: For each high-mismatch sensitivity sequence, the envelope identifies the macroscopic assignment mixtures that need an exact or smaller-order selection criterion.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the multivariate van Trees result used for the nuisance-adjusted information lower bound that exposes the complete first-order face.

open_obligations.what_is_open: A necessary-and-sufficient contact characterization of \(\mathcal Q^*_{\infty}[(s_J)]\) inside \(\mathcal F_\rho\) that recovers limits by exact finite minimizers for every sequence with \(s_J/J\to\rho\ge1/2\).
open_obligations.obstruction: The first-order lower game is flat on \(\mathcal F_\rho\), while the frozen limiting-experiment handle specifies no local scaling, limiting kernel, second-order risk, or uniform epiconvergence theorem. The exact finite conic certificates determine every fixed \(J\) but do not by themselves identify which contact points persist under \(J\to\infty\), especially when \(s_J-J/2\) changes on a smaller scale.
open_obligations.attempted: The scalar and two-parameter shrinking-prior experiments were solved, including singular boundary information, and matched by a balanced-orbit centered estimator. They yield the sharp value and the exact first-order envelope. Expanding the resulting information game cannot distinguish two measures with the same balance and mean-mixed constraints; replacing exact minimizers by \(o(J^{-1})\)-optimal procedures therefore loses precisely the selection information requested by the OEQ.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The exact finite contact system of Theorem 1 makes every set \(\mathcal Q^*(J,s_J)\) computable, and Theorem 5 proves
\[
 \mathcal Q^*_{\infty}[(s_J)]\subseteq\mathcal F_\rho.
\]
It also recovers every \(\mu\in\mathcal F_\rho\) by procedures whose excess worst risk is \(o(J^{-1})\). The unresolved distinction is precisely replacement of those first-order procedures by exact finite minimizers.
